# Preface {.unnumbered}

This thesis is the result of four and a half years of PhD, during which I had the opportunity to work on many aspects of gravitational wave astronomy. 
Its first two chapters take the reader through the details of how we can go from the data observed by a detector to the properties of the astrophysical source which generated the signal.

@sec-statistical-methods introduces the statistical tools required to efficiently perform inference; 
these are of general applicability, though the discussion already has an eye toward gravitational waves.
@sec-gw-pe illustrates how these tools can be applied to gravitational waves specifically, 
_i.e._ to the robust analysis of timeseries, as well as what computational acceleration techniques 
can be applied at this stage.

The next three chapters summarize the main effects which can drive variations in the waveform measured at the detectors.
In @sec-gw250114 we introduce the protagonist signal for this endeavour is introduced, GW250114, which as of this writing
holds the record as the clearest-ever gravitational wave detection. 
In @sec-intrinsic we outline how the signal produced by a binary compact merger is characterized, while in @sec-extrinsic
we take it from the source to the detector, by discussing the geometric relation between us and the emitter.

Finally, in @sec-einstein-telescope and @sec-lgwa we look toward the next decades 
with two concepts for future detectors, both of which are developing 
thriving collaborations. 

This thesis is simultaneously compiled with [quarto](https://quarto.org/) 
into both HTML --- as a static website --- and PDF.
The HTML version is interactive, with hyperlinks, the possibility to see
internal and external references by mouse over, and a dynamic table of contents.
Also, several figures are rendered from `python` code, 
which can be seen directly within the website, but is omitted from the PDF.
This literate programming-like approach [@knuthLiterateProgramming1984] 
allows for reproducibility and transparency.
I would like thesis to be a "living document" of sorts, 
which I can keep updating after graduation.
